corrections.text: M42.5 treated `harness.module_import` as an import observation and inferred from it that the security module itself failed to load.  It was a renaming of `Get-Command Get-AuthenticodeSignature`, and the probe's real import ran under -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue into Out-Null, so no import outcome was ever captured.  M42.6 separated the observations and republished them under names that cannot be confused; no published record was reinterpreted and no schema version changed, because the harness subfields carry no promised meaning

observations: the restored-sandbox pattern repeated: the local object store lost commits that the remote had, while the worktree kept their content; recovery therefore means fingerprinting content, adopting the remote tip non-destructively, and committing the delta - never re-creating history

a gate that fails twice for the same reason is not flaky noise: the second failure produced the observation (listed at the check, refused at the exec) that the first could not, because the instrumentation added between them was designed to attribute rather than to hide

the signing UNKNOWN, the capability-probe remedy, the retry and the artifact-transport blocker are four separate findings and must not be merged into one story: only the first two concern the signature record, and the fourth prevents anyone from claiming the bytes were verified here

a field name is part of the evidence: `module_import` held an availability answer, and every document that read it as an import observation inherited that error - naming and prose had to be corrected together

a mutation battery's survivors are the most useful output it produces: four of them were gaps in this mission's own tests, and two were documents that still allowed the old inference to be read back in

attribution_correction.defect: `$imported = [bool](Get-Command Get-AuthenticodeSignature ...)` and `module_import=$(if ($imported) { 'succeeded' } else { 'failed' })`, while `Import-Module Microsoft.PowerShell.Security -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Out-Null` threw the only real import evidence away
attribution_correction.why_it_mattered: a record could claim the module import failed while proving only that the command did not resolve, and the prose around it did exactly that; the two facts also implied different remedies - a runner-image change versus a build change
attribution_correction.decision_table: import succeeded + cmdlet available -> the per-file answer; import failed + cmdlet available -> the per-file answer with the anomaly recorded beside it; cmdlet unavailable (either import outcome) -> UNKNOWN with that cause and nothing else; probe unusable -> the per-file answer if the queries answered, with probe_usable=false
attribution_correction.never_permitted: an import or probe observation may not produce UNSIGNED, PASS or FAIL, and a missing cmdlet is never a statement about the files
attribution_correction.schema_decision: no version bump: `harness` subfields are unconstrained host observations in drillmaster-signing-status/v2, the new keys are additive, and the retired key is left undeclared rather than redefined so older records still mean what they literally said

lifecycle_instability_observed.what_happened: the next records-only commit, 6c4979fce0abdef9a2823889345d24aa78ddef93, whose code and workflow are byte-identical to the gated SHA (its delta is four record and guard paths), produced a Windows run in which the lifecycle step failed: installed_files PASS, installed_version PASS, installed_smoke PASS with the install tree unchanged, data_outside_install_dir PASS, then silent_uninstall FAIL reading 'attempt 1: unins000.exe was listed but could not be launched (FileNotFoundError: [WinError 2] ...); install tree holds 0 file(s): nothing' and the second attempt after the two-second settle likewise refused
lifecycle_instability_observed.what_it_proves: the install tree had emptied entirely between the smoke step's post-check and the uninstall - an external removal under the runner's own _temp root - which is the condition the retry was built to survive and the condition the second-refusal rule is built to fail on. The protections worked as specified; the environment did not cooperate
lifecycle_instability_observed.what_it_does_not_prove: nothing about the packaging being wrong: the same bytes reached lifecycle=PASS on the previous commit, and no code changed between them. Nor does it identify the agent that removed the tree - attributing it to antivirus real-time protection would be a guess, and it stays one
lifecycle_instability_observed.response: no threshold, retry count, empty-directory proof or second-refusal failure was relaxed. The run was reported as a failed gate for that SHA, the step-by-step conclusions were read back and recorded, and REL-13 was added to the acceptance register so the instability is an owner-visible obligation rather than a footnote. A re-run of the identical SHA was attempted first and is refused by this installation's permissions (the rerun and dispatch endpoints both answer 403 Resource not accessible by integration), so the only available route to a green Windows gate on a tip is another commit, which is why this record commit is followed by its own read-back in the mission report
lifecycle_instability_observed.consequence_for_the_verdict: the release-engineering verdict is anchored on the code SHA, where both gates are green; the records tip's Windows result is stated as it was observed, and any claim that the final published SHA has both gates green must come from a run of that SHA, not from this paragraph

lifecycle_instability_investigation.question: why did the installed-application lifecycle step pass on one SHA and fail the next on byte-identical packaging code, and can a repeatable code defect be told apart from a runner or external filesystem event?
lifecycle_instability_investigation.what_the_published_record_could_not_say: snapshot() returns an empty mapping both when a directory is missing and when it is present but empty, so the published 'install tree holds 0 file(s): nothing' could not distinguish a removed tree from an emptied one; and evidence['diagnostics']['uninstall_log'] was written only after the runner returned, so the record could not show whether any uninstaller process had run at all
lifecycle_instability_investigation.timeline_established_from_the_failing_ru: installed_files PASS, installed_version PASS, installed_smoke PASS reporting an unchanged install tree, data_outside_install_dir PASS with the sentinel write under work_root/userdata succeeding, so the work root existed and was writable immediately before the refusal; the pre-check uninstaller.is_file() then returned True and the launch still raised WinError 2
lifecycle_instability_investigation.reasoning_kept_separate_from_evidence: a missing working directory would surface as WinError 267 rather than 2, which argues against a vanished cwd; that is labelled as an inference, and the samples added by this mission are what replaces it with direct evidence
lifecycle_instability_investigation.classification: runner or external filesystem event on that host, cause undetermined at the permissions the gate has. No code defect was found in the lifecycle logic, and the failure did not reproduce: the next two exact-SHA runs of the same code passed every lifecycle step, which is why no fix is claimed
lifecycle_instability_investigation.repeatability_limit: the same SHA cannot be re-run from this workspace: POST rerun, rerun-failed-jobs and workflow_dispatch each return 403 for this installation, and gh run rerun reports that the workflow file may be broken.
